claim: Pack covers bubbles, Depression, stagflation, 2008, told from primary sources

edits.old: Four episodes that still shape how economies are run: the first great bubbles, the Great Depression, 1970s stagflation, and the 2008 financial crisis, told from primary sources.
edits.new: Four episodes that still shape how economies are run: the first great bubbles, the Great Depression, 1970s stagflation, and the 2008 financial crisis, told from official sources.

note: Cited pages are Fed/Treasury/FDIC histories and letters written decades later (secondary accounts), not primary historical sources. Episodes list matches the four topics.

edits.new: How a stock market crash was followed by a decade-long slump: bank runs, a shrinking money supply, the gold standard, the 1933 bank holiday, and the reforms that followed.

note: "Became" states the crash caused the Depression; the cited essay stresses banking panics and the money-supply collapse. Sequence wording avoids overstating a contested causal link.

claim: Tulips reached Western Europe from Turkey; fourth-largest Dutch export by 1636; bulb worth an Amsterdam house Jan 1637

edits.old: Tulips reached Western Europe from Turkey in the 1600s and quickly became a status symbol in the Netherlands, prized because they were rare and beautiful. Bulbs that produced flowers with streaked, flame-like petals were valued far above plain single-colour ones. A market for bulbs developed, growers began bidding prices up, and buyers who had never grown a flower joined in, hoping to resell at a profit.
edits.new: Tulips reached Western Europe from Turkey in the late 1500s and by the early 1600s had become a status symbol in the Netherlands, prized because they were rare and beautiful. Bulbs that produced flowers with streaked, flame-like petals were valued far above plain single-color ones. A market for bulbs developed, growers began bidding prices up, and buyers who had never grown a flower joined in, hoping to resell at a profit.

edits.old: By 1636 tulip bulbs had become the fourth-largest export of the Netherlands. By January 1637 a single rare bulb was valued at about the price of one of the finest houses in Amsterdam. The flower had not changed; only the number of people expecting to resell it had.
edits.new: One Fed account says that by 1636 tulip bulbs had become the fourth-largest export of the Netherlands. By January 1637 a single rare bulb was valued at about the price of one of the finest houses in Amsterdam. The flower had not changed; only the number of people expecting to resell it had.

note: Tulips arrived in Western Europe in the 16th century (Clusius planted them at Leiden in 1593); the source says only that they were new in the 1600s. "colour" to US spelling. Export ranking is disputed by historians, so attributed.

claim: Futures and options markets developed once tulip prices rose, allowing bets without possession
note: Source explicitly says "futures" and "options" markets developed once prices rose, letting investors bet without taking possession. Resale-chain example is a fair illustration.

claim: Tulip market collapsed February 1637 as speculators pulled out

edits.old: In February 1637 buyers stepped back from Dutch tulip bulbs. Sellers rushed to get out before prices fell further, and the market collapsed entirely. Bulbs valued weeks earlier at the price of an Amsterdam mansion found no one willing to pay anything close, because the only reason to pay had been the next buyer.
edits.new: In February 1637 buyers stepped back from Dutch tulip bulbs. Sellers rushed to get out before prices fell further, and the market collapsed. Bulbs valued weeks earlier at the price of an Amsterdam mansion found no buyer near that price. Historians still debate how far the losses spread beyond the traders directly involved.

note: Feb 1637 collapse confirmed. "Only reason to pay had been the next buyer" overstated; rare bulbs kept some value, and Garber/Goldgar dispute the scale of wider damage. Added one balancing sentence.

claim: Bank of England opened 1 Aug 1694 to fund war with France; South Sea Company 1711 targeted debt servicing

edits.old: The Bank of England opened for business on 1 August 1694, founded chiefly to pay for the war against France. Seventeen years later, in 1711, the South Sea Company was created and set its sights on the same job of servicing the national debt, the work that had largely been the Bank's.
edits.new: The Bank of England opened for business on August 1, 1694, founded chiefly to pay for the war against France. Seventeen years later, in 1711, the South Sea Company was created and set its sights on the same job of servicing the national debt, the work that had largely been the Bank's.

note: Facts match the Bank of England page (opened 1 Aug 1694; South Sea Company 1711; 17-year gap correct). Date changed to the U.S. month-day-year style used on every other pack card.

claim: 1720 South Sea Company granted part of national debt; stock rose dramatically, crashed, thousands ruined
note: Matches Bank of England page wording on the 1720 debt grant, frenzy, crash and ruin; whole cycle within 1720 is consistent with the record (peak mid-1720, collapse by autumn).

claim: "Bubble" coined 1720; copycat schemes; Bubble Act 1720; scheme whose purpose nobody knew

edits.old: One scheme of 1720 advertised itself as a venture of great advantage whose purpose nobody was allowed to know, and still found subscribers. The Bubble Act passed the same year. The pattern of a genuine boom surrounded by fraud recurred in later episodes; the 1720 case simply gave it a name.
edits.new: One scheme of 1720 reportedly advertised itself as a venture of great advantage whose purpose nobody was allowed to know, and still found subscribers. The Bubble Act passed in June 1720, before the crash rather than after it. The pattern of a genuine boom surrounded by fraud recurred in later episodes; the 1720 case simply gave it a name.

note: Letter confirms coinage, Bubble Act and the scheme quote. The scheme story traces to Mackay (1841) and is unverified, hence "reportedly". The Act received royal assent June 1720, before the autumn crash; card implied it followed.

claim: Banking Act signed June 16 1933; temporary fund Jan 1 1934 at $2,500; $5,000 from July 1934; separation repealed 1999

claim: Aug 15 1971: gold convertibility at $35 ended, 90-day freeze, 10% import surcharge; Bretton Woods 1944

edits.old: Under the Bretton Woods system, designed in 1944, foreign governments could exchange U.S. dollars for gold at a fixed price, and other currencies were pegged to the dollar. Closing the gold window meant the United States stopped honouring that exchange. Without the gold anchor, currencies moved to floating rates set by markets, and the dollar's value depended on confidence rather than a metal.

claim: 1971 controls ran in phases to 1974, slowed prices temporarily, worsened shortages; inflation over 12% in 1974

edits.old: The controls announced in 1971 ran in 3 phases until 1974. They slowed price rises only temporarily and made shortages worse, especially for food and energy. Once they lapsed, the delayed increases arrived: inflation exceeded 12 percent in 1974, higher than before the freeze began.
edits.new: The controls announced in 1971 ran in a series of phases until April 1974. They slowed price rises only temporarily and made shortages worse, especially for food and energy. After they lapsed, with an oil shock also under way, inflation exceeded 12 percent in 1974, far higher than before the freeze began.

note: Essay says "three phases", but the program had Phases I-IV plus a second 1973 freeze, ending April 1974. Card blamed 1974 inflation solely on controls lapsing; the 1973-74 oil shock (stg-003) was a major cause.

claim: Recession July 1981-Nov 1982; unemployment near 11% postwar high; inflation 11% to 5%; 90% of job losses goods sector; 22%/24%

edits.old: The recession ran from July 1981 to November 1982. Unemployment neared 11 percent at the end of 1982, the postwar high, while inflation fell from 11 percent in June 1979 to 5 percent by October 1982. Goods-producing sectors took 90 percent of the job losses in 1982; unemployment reached 22 percent in residential construction and 24 percent in auto manufacturing.
edits.new: The recession ran from July 1981 to November 1982. Unemployment neared 11 percent at the end of 1982, then the highest since World War II, while inflation fell from 11 percent in June 1979 to 5 percent by October 1982. Goods-producing sectors took 90 percent of the job losses in 1982; unemployment reached 22 percent in residential construction and 24 percent in auto manufacturing.

note: Essay written 2013 says it "remains the apex"; unemployment reached 14.8% in April 2020, so no longer the postwar high. Other figures match; CPI-U June 1979 10.9%, Oct 1982 5.1% (BLS).

claim: Coverage $250,000 per depositor, bank, ownership category; no insured loss since 1933

edits.old: Deposit insurance removes the reason to run on a bank: if the bank fails, the insurer pays depositors up to the limit, so there is nothing to gain by pulling money out first. Coverage is counted per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category, so one person can be covered separately for a single account, a joint account, and a retirement account at the same bank.
edits.new: Deposit insurance removes the reason to run on a bank: if the bank fails, the insurer pays depositors up to the limit, so there is nothing to gain by pulling money out first. The promise works only if depositors trust it, which is why the U.S. coverage limit was raised during the 2008 crisis.

edits.old: The FDIC was founded in 1933, and since then no depositor has lost a penny of insured funds. The standard limit is $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. A saver with $250,000 in a single account and $250,000 in a joint account at 1 bank is fully covered on both.
edits.new: In October 2008, in the middle of the crisis, Congress raised the standard coverage limit to $250,000, at first only until the end of 2009. The Dodd-Frank Act of July 2010 then made the $250,000 limit permanent.
